claim: muse11-1 and muse11-2 enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in mos snc1 backgrounds, including stunted growth.
source: As with all other muse mutants, both muse11 alleles enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in the mos snc1 backgrounds, including stunted growth (Figure 1A), elevated defence marker Pathogenesis Related (PR) gene expression (Figure 1B) and enhanced disease resistance against the virulent oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (H.a.) Noco2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating the stunted growth phenotype.

claim: muse11-1 and muse11-2 enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in mos snc1 backgrounds, including elevated defence marker Pathogenesis Related (PR) gene expression.
source: As with all other muse mutants, both muse11 alleles enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in the mos snc1 backgrounds, including stunted growth (Figure 1A), elevated defence marker Pathogenesis Related (PR) gene expression (Figure 1B) and enhanced disease resistance against the virulent oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (H.a.) Noco2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating elevated PR gene expression.

claim: muse11-1 and muse11-2 enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in mos snc1 backgrounds, including enhanced disease resistance against the virulent oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (H.a.) Noco2.
source: As with all other muse mutants, both muse11 alleles enhance snc1-mediated autoimmunity in the mos snc1 backgrounds, including stunted growth (Figure 1A), elevated defence marker Pathogenesis Related (PR) gene expression (Figure 1B) and enhanced disease resistance against the virulent oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (H.a.) Noco2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating enhanced disease resistance.

claim: muse11-1 and muse11-2 are recessive mutations.
source: When the isolated mutants were backcrossed with mos snc1 parents, the F1 plants were mos snc1-like, indicating that muse11-1 and muse11-2 are recessive.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic data from backcross experiments showing F1 plants resemble the wild-type parent.

claim: muse11-1 and muse11-2 likely carry mutations in the same gene.
source: When muse11-1 mos4 snc1 was crossed with muse11-2 mos2 snc1 npr1, all F1 progeny showed dwarfism similar to both parent lines, indicating failed complementation (Figure 1D). Therefore muse11-1 and muse11-2 likely carry mutations in the same gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic complementation test data showing failed complementation in F1 progeny.

claim: MUSE11 is AT5G42950.
source: Comparison of the genome re-sequenced muse11-1 mos4 snc1 and muse11-2 mos2 snc1 npr1 sequences in the muse11 region revealed different mutations in only one common gene, AT5G42950 (Figure 2B), which were not present in either the mos4 snc1 or mos2 snc1 npr1 parent line. Sequence analysis revealed that the two muse11 alleles harbour different early stop codon mutations, presumably causing truncations of the encoded protein (Figure 2B). Therefore MUSE11 is most likely AT5G42950.
evidence: The claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data identifying mutations in AT5G42950 in both muse11 alleles.

claim: AT5G42950 was recently named as EXA1 (Essential for poteXvirus Accumulation).
source: This gene was recently named as EXA1 (Essential for poteXvirus Accumulation), as loss of EXA1 causes enhanced resistance to viruses (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication.

claim: Loss of EXA1 causes enhanced resistance to viruses.
source: This gene was recently named as EXA1 (Essential for poteXvirus Accumulation), as loss of EXA1 causes enhanced resistance to viruses (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication.

claim: exa1-1 greatly enhanced the snc1 phenotypes as the muse11 alleles.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, exa1-1 greatly enhanced the snc1 phenotypes as the muse11 alleles.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating phenotypic enhancement.

claim: Both exa1-1 and exa1-2 single mutant plants are smaller in size compared with WT.
source: Both exa1-1 and exa1-2 single mutant plants are smaller in size compared with WT and display a curly leaf phenotype similar to snc1, suggestive of autoimmunity (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating plant size differences.

claim: exa1-1 and exa1-2 display a curly leaf phenotype similar to snc1, suggestive of autoimmunity.
source: Both exa1-1 and exa1-2 single mutant plants are smaller in size compared with WT and display a curly leaf phenotype similar to snc1, suggestive of autoimmunity (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and inference about autoimmunity based on phenotypic similarity.

claim: The expression of PR1 and PR2 is significantly increased in both exa1-1 and exa1-2 plants.
source: RT-PCR analysis showed that the expression of PR1 and PR2 is significantly increased in both exa1-1 and exa1-2 plants (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both exa1-1 and exa1-2 alleles cause enhanced resistance against H.a. Noco2.
source: When challenged with virulent pathogens, both alleles cause enhanced resistance against H.a. Noco2 and bacteria Pseudomonas syringae pv. maculicola (P.s.m.) ES4326 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathogen infection assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both exa1-1 and exa1-2 alleles cause enhanced resistance against bacteria Pseudomonas syringae pv. maculicola (P.s.m.) ES4326.
source: When challenged with virulent pathogens, both alleles cause enhanced resistance against H.a. Noco2 and bacteria Pseudomonas syringae pv. maculicola (P.s.m.) ES4326 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathogen infection assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EXA1 plays a negative role in immunity.
source: Collectively, these phenotypic analyses of the knockout mutants indicate that EXA1 plays a negative role in immunity; loss of EXA1 leads to enhanced resistance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotypic analyses showing enhanced resistance in exa1 mutants.

claim: Loss of EXA1 leads to enhanced resistance.
source: Collectively, these phenotypic analyses of the knockout mutants indicate that EXA1 plays a negative role in immunity; loss of EXA1 leads to enhanced resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analyses of exa1 mutants showing enhanced resistance to pathogens.

claim: EXA1 encodes a large protein of 1714 amino acids.
source: Protein sequence analysis showed that EXA1 encodes a large protein of 1714 amino acids, with a predicted eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binding motif and a glycine-tyrosine-phenylalanine (GYF) domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence analysis.

claim: EXA1 has a predicted eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binding motif.
source: Protein sequence analysis showed that EXA1 encodes a large protein of 1714 amino acids, with a predicted eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binding motif and a glycine-tyrosine-phenylalanine (GYF) domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence analysis and prediction.

claim: EXA1 has a glycine-tyrosine-phenylalanine (GYF) domain.
source: Protein sequence analysis showed that EXA1 encodes a large protein of 1714 amino acids, with a predicted eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) binding motif and a glycine-tyrosine-phenylalanine (GYF) domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence analysis.

claim: GYF domains are molecular adaptors that bind to proline-rich sequences.
source: GYF domains are molecular adaptors that bind to proline-rich sequences (Kofler and Freund, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to established knowledge.

claim: The GYF domain in EXA1 is composed of 57 amino acid residues from position 546–603, close to its N-terminus.
source: The GYF domain in EXA1 is composed of 57 amino acid residues from position 546–603, close to its N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by protein sequence analysis.

claim: GYF domains are found in all eukaryotes.

claim: EXA1 full-length protein putative orthologs are restricted to the plant lineage.
source: However, when EXA1 full-length protein was analyzed, its putative orthologs are restricted to the plant lineage (Figure 4C).

claim: There are eight GYF domain-containing proteins in Arabidopsis.

claim: The SWIB/PHD/GYF clade proteins, exemplified by NERD (Needed for RDR2-independent DNA methylation; AT2G16485), seem to be involved in transcription and chromatin modifications, participating in chromatin-based RNA silencing.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The roles of the EXA1 clade proteins in plants remain elusive.
source: However, the roles of the EXA1 clade proteins in plants remain elusive.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: AT1G24300 and AT1G27430, the two closest paralogs of EXA1, share 45% and 43% sequence similarity with EXA1, respectively.
source: AT1G24300 and AT1G27430, the two closest paralogs of EXA1, share 45% and 43% sequence similarity with EXA1, respectively (Figure 5A).

claim: AT1G24300 and AT1G27430 have likely evolved independently from EXA1.
source: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that these two genes likely have evolved independently from EXA1 (Figure 4C).

claim: Homozygous exonic T-DNA alleles of AT1G24300 (SALK_ 058114) and AT1G27430 (SALK_035304) are indistinguishable from WT.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Double mutant plants of AT1G24300 (SALK_ 058114) and AT1G27430 (SALK_035304) with snc1 display snc1-like morphology.
source: As shown in Figure 5C and D, homozygous exonic T-DNA alleles of AT1G24300 (SALK_ 058114) and AT1G27430 (SALK_035304) are indistinguishable from WT and their double mutant plants with snc1 display snc1-like morphology.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: EXA1 seems to be a single-copy gene involved in the negative regulation of plant immunity.
source: Taken together, EXA1 seems to be a single-copy gene involved in the negative regulation of plant immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of functional redundancy with paralogs and the phenotypic data.

claim: EXA1 is predicted to localize to the chloroplast on The Arabidopsis Information Resource (TAIR).

claim: No transmembrane domains or nuclear localization signals were found in EXA1.

claim: EXA1-GFP largely complemented the autoimmune phenotypes of exa1-2, including enhanced resistance to H.a. Noco2 and P.s.m. ES4326.

evidence: The claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: EXA1-GFP is functional.
source: As shown in Figure 6, EXA1-GFP largely complemented the autoimmune phenotypes of exa1-2, including stunted growth (Figure 6A) and enhanced resistance to H.a. Noco2 and P.s.m. ES4326 (6B and 6C), suggesting that EXA1-GFP is functional and likely localizes to its native sites.

claim: EXA1 is unlikely to be involved in mRNA splicing as with CD2BP2.
source: Confocal microscopy examination revealed that EXA1-GFP localizes to the cytosol, but is absent from the nucleus of Arabidopsis root cells (Figure 6E), indicating that EXA1 is unlikely to be involved in mRNA splicing as with CD2BP2.

claim: EXA1 may play other roles, such as translational control, as with SMY2.
source: Rather, it may play other roles, such as translational control, as with SMY2.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on similarity to SMY2 and cytosolic localization.

source: In agreement with this observation, the GYF domain in EXA1 is more similar to SMY2 than with CD2BP2 (Figure 4B).

claim: Significantly increased SNC1 levels were consistently observed in both exa1-1 and exa1-2 single mutant plants compared with WT.

claim: Much higher SNC1 protein levels were detected in the exa1-1 snc1 double mutant when compared with snc1.
source: Similarly, immunoblot analysis detected much higher SNC1 protein levels in the exa1-1 snc1 double mutant when compared with snc1 (Figure 7A and B), although the expression of SNC1 is not affected (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The expression of SNC1 is not affected in exa1-1 snc1 double mutant compared with snc1.
source: Similarly, immunoblot analysis detected much higher SNC1 protein levels in the exa1-1 snc1 double mutant when compared with snc1 (Figure 7A and B), although the expression of SNC1 is not affected (Figure 7C).

claim: EXA1 regulates SNC1 protein accumulation, likely through translational events.

claim: The overexpression of EXA1 renders lower SNC1 levels when SNC1-HA was co-infiltrated with EXA1-FLAG in Nicotiana benthamiana.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SNC1 transcript levels were not affected by EXA1 overexpression in Nicotiana benthamiana.
source: Importantly, SNC1 transcript levels were not affected by EXA1 overexpression (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Overexpression of the functional EXA1-FLAG in snc1 partially suppresses the dwarf stature of snc1.
source: Consistent with the observations in tobacco, overexpression of the functional EXA1-FLAG in snc1 partially suppresses the dwarf stature of snc1 (Figure 7F) without affecting SNC1 transcript levels (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Overexpression of EXA1-FLAG in snc1 does not affect SNC1 transcript levels.
source: Consistent with the observations in tobacco, overexpression of the functional EXA1-FLAG in snc1 partially suppresses the dwarf stature of snc1 (Figure 7F) without affecting SNC1 transcript levels (Figure 7G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: EXA1-FLAG overexpression reduces the accumulation of SNC1.

evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: The autoimmunity of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 was partially suppressed by snc1-r1.
source: The autoimmunity of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 was also partially suppressed by snc1-r1 (Figure 8C), indicating that the enhanced immunity of exa1 is only partially dependent on SNC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathogen infection assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The enhanced immunity of exa1 is only partially dependent on SNC1.
source: The autoimmunity of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 was also partially suppressed by snc1-r1 (Figure 8C), indicating that the enhanced immunity of exa1 is only partially dependent on SNC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the partial suppression of exa1-1 autoimmunity by snc1-r1.

claim: The size, fresh weight and enhanced resistance of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 were only partially suppressed by the loss of EDS1.
source: As shown in Figure 8A–C, the size, fresh weight and enhanced resistance of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 were only partially suppressed by the loss of EDS1, indicating that EXA1 may also affect additional EDS1-independent NLRs.
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic and pathogen infection assay data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: EXA1 may also affect additional EDS1-independent NLRs.
source: As shown in Figure 8A–C, the size, fresh weight and enhanced resistance of exa1-1 against H.a. Noco2 were only partially suppressed by the loss of EDS1, indicating that EXA1 may also affect additional EDS1-independent NLRs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the partial suppression of exa1-1 phenotypes by eds1.

claim: The over-accumulation of SNC1 in exa1 is only partially responsible for its enhanced resistance phenotype.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the over-accumulation of SNC1 in exa1 is only partially responsible for its enhanced resistance phenotype.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic data showing partial suppression by snc1-r1 and eds1.

claim: All three NLRs (RPS4-HA, RPM1-Myc, and RPS2-HA) accumulated to significantly higher levels in exa1-1.
source: Interestingly, all three NLRs accumulated to significantly higher levels in exa1-1 (Figure 9A–C), although their transcript levels are not affected (Figure 9D–F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that EXA1 has a general role in negatively controlling NLR protein accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: The transcript levels of RPS4, RPM1, and RPS2 are not affected in exa1-1.
source: Interestingly, all three NLRs accumulated to significantly higher levels in exa1-1 (Figure 9A–C), although their transcript levels are not affected (Figure 9D–F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that EXA1 has a general role in negatively controlling NLR protein accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 9D-F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: EXA1 has a general role in negatively controlling NLR protein accumulation.
source: Interestingly, all three NLRs accumulated to significantly higher levels in exa1-1 (Figure 9A–C), although their transcript levels are not affected (Figure 9D–F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that EXA1 has a general role in negatively controlling NLR protein accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that multiple NLRs accumulate to higher levels in exa1-1 without changes in transcript levels.

claim: Reduced bacterial growth of both Pst DC3000 AvrRps4 and Pst DC3000 AvrRpm1 was observed in the exa1 single mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 9G–H, reduced bacterial growth of both Pst DC3000 AvrRps4 and Pst DC3000 AvrRpm1 was observed in the exa1 single mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 9G-H.

claim: No enhanced resistance against Pst DC3000 AvrRpt2 was observed in exa1 single mutants even though heightened RPS2 protein level was detected.
source: However, even though heightened RPS2 protein level was detected in the exa1 single mutant plants (Figure 9C), no enhanced resistance against Pst DC3000 AvrRpt2 was observed (Figure 9I).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 9I and Western blot data in Figure 9C.

claim: It is possible that the threshold for achieving resistance against AvrRpt2 is higher than the accumulated RPS2 in the exa1 single mutant.
source: It is possible that the threshold for achieving resistance against AvrRpt2 is higher than the accumulated RPS2 in the exa1 single mutant.
evidence: The claim is speculative, attempting to explain the lack of enhanced resistance despite increased RPS2 levels.

claim: Besides SNC1, EXA1 also contributes to the accumulation of other NLRs including RPS4, RPS2 and RPM1.
source: Taken together, besides SNC1, EXA1 also contributes to the accumulation of other NLRs including RPS4, RPS2 and RPM1.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased levels of these NLRs in exa1 mutants.

claim: A slight increase in FLS2 was observed in the exa1 mutants.
source: From western blot analyses, we observed a slight increase in FLS2, but not significant difference in EFR and BAK1 protein levels in the exa1 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–C).

claim: No significant difference in EFR and BAK1 protein levels was observed in the exa1 mutants.
source: From western blot analyses, we observed a slight increase in FLS2, but not significant difference in EFR and BAK1 protein levels in the exa1 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The protein levels of MOS4 and MOS12 are comparable to that in the WT background.
source: The protein levels of MOS4 and MOS12 are comparable to that in the WT background (Figure 9—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: The H3, but not HSP70s, shows significant accumulation in exa1 mutants.
source: Interestingly, the H3, but not HSP70s, shows significant accumulation in exa1 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: EXA1 does not seem to influence general protein synthesis.
source: Taken together, EXA1 does not seem to influence general protein synthesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that not all proteins tested show increased accumulation in exa1 mutants.

claim: Besides NLRs, EXA1 also negatively impacts accumulation of other proteins such as FLS2 and H3.
source: Besides NLRs, it also negatively impacts accumulation of other proteins such as FLS2 and H3.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased levels of FLS2 and H3 in exa1 mutants.

claim: EXA1 interacts strongly with RPL18 in split-luciferase complementation assay.
source: As shown in Figure 10A and B, EXA1 indeed interacts strongly with RPL18.
evidence: The claim is supported by split-luciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: RPL18-HA efficiently pulled down EXA1-FLAG in N. benthamiana leaves which transiently expressed EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA.
source: We further performed immunoprecipiration assays in N. benthamiana leaves which transiently expressed EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA, and in Arabidopsis plants stably transformed with both EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA. In both cases, RPL18-HA efficiently pulled down EXA1-FLAG (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: RPL18-HA efficiently pulled down EXA1-FLAG in Arabidopsis plants stably transformed with both EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA.
source: We further performed immunoprecipiration assays in N. benthamiana leaves which transiently expressed EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA, and in Arabidopsis plants stably transformed with both EXA1-FLAG and RPL18-HA. In both cases, RPL18-HA efficiently pulled down EXA1-FLAG (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Stronger luciferase activity was observed when C-Luc-EXA1 was co-infiltrated with eIF4E1-NLuc.
source: As EXA1 was predicted to contain a conserved motif for interaction with eIF4E, we also tested for interactions between EXA1 and eIF4E1 or eIF4E1B. Stronger luciferase activity was observed when C-Luc-EXA1 was co-infiltrated with eIF4E1-NLuc or eIF4E1B (Figure 10E and F), confirming the predicted interaction with the initiation factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by split-luciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Stronger luciferase activity was observed when C-Luc-EXA1 was co-infiltrated with eIF4E1B.
source: As EXA1 was predicted to contain a conserved motif for interaction with eIF4E, we also tested for interactions between EXA1 and eIF4E1 or eIF4E1B. Stronger luciferase activity was observed when C-Luc-EXA1 was co-infiltrated with eIF4E1-NLuc or eIF4E1B (Figure 10E and F), confirming the predicted interaction with the initiation factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by split-luciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: The interaction between C-Luc-EXA1 and mature SNC1-N-Luc was not detectable.
source: Interestingly, the interaction between C-Luc-EXA1 and mature SNC1-N-Luc was not detectable (Figure 10G), suggesting that EXA1 does not function at the termination step of translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by split-luciferase complementation assay data shown in Figure 10G.

claim: EXA1 does not function at the termination step of translation.
source: Interestingly, the interaction between C-Luc-EXA1 and mature SNC1-N-Luc was not detectable (Figure 10G), suggesting that EXA1 does not function at the termination step of translation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of detectable interaction between EXA1 and mature SNC1.

claim: EXA1 is indeed associating with ribosomes and translational initiation factors, likely through translational repression of NLRs.
source: Together, these data confirm the sequence prediction that EXA1 is indeed associating with ribosomes and translational initiation factors, likely through translational repression of NLRs, as knocking out EXA1 leads to NLR accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by interaction data with RPL18 and eIF4E factors, and inferred from the accumulation of NLRs in exa1 mutants.

claim: Plant NLRs are under tight negative control through regulating appropriate NLR gene expression at the chromatin level.
source: To avoid autoimmunity, plant NLRs are under tight negative control through: (1) regulating appropriate NLR gene expression at the chromatin level (Johnson et al., 2012, 2015), (2) proper alternative splicing of NLR mRNAs at the posttranscriptional level (Johnson et al., 2016), (3) coordination of N-terminal acetylation during NLR protein synthesis (Xu et al., 2015), and (4) post-translationally maintaining NLR protein homeostasis via the ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation pathway (Cheng et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2014a, 2014b, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Plant NLRs are under tight negative control through proper alternative splicing of NLR mRNAs at the posttranscriptional level.
